I’ve read every book on this list and chose them because I still can’t stop thinking about them. I'm not alone in finding these works to be transformative: all but two of the books below have been adapted for television or the stage. Without further ado, here are the best books of the last 30 years.

10
'Persepolis' by Marjane Satrapi (2000)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/persepolis-book-cover.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
Image via Pantheon Books

Marjane Satrapi literally draws us a picture of growing up in Iran during the 1979 Islamic Revolution and the Iran-Iraq War. She is funny, stubborn, political, frightened, and occasionally ridiculous in exactly the ways children are. One minute, she's trying to understand the revolution and martyrdom that's disrupting her childhood; the next, she is worried about Western music and getting caught in the wrong clothes (such as a rhinestone-beadazzled jean jacket à la "Thriller"-era Michael Jackson). Those shifts make the world around her feel immediate.

Governments fall. Wars begin. People disappear. Children still want cool sneakers. That tension between history and ordinary childhood is what makesPersepolisstay with me. In 2007, Satrapi and director Vincent Paronnaud adapted her novel into a film of the same name and won the Jury Prize at the 2007 Cannes Film Festival.What I haven’t stopped thinking about: the way Satrapi changes the size of God’s head depending on his influence in Marji’s life. A drawn bracelet in the rubble from a bombing signals that her friend is dead.

9
'The Year of Magical Thinking' by Joan Didion (2005)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/joan-didion-social-featured.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
Image via IMDb

While their daughter, Quintana Roo Dunne, is critically ill in the hospital, Joan Didion’s husband, John Gregory Dunne, suddenly dies at their dinner table. The Year of Magical Thinking is about living inside grief rather than examining it from some safe distance. Didion knows her husband is dead. She also cannot put away his shoes because he might need them when he comes back.

She cannot read his obituary because everyone keeps referring to him as dead. That is the terrible logic of grief: maybe if you keep returning to the moment, asking the same questions, the ending will change. Grief rearranges logic until knowing something and accepting it become entirely different things. In 2007, David Hare adapted Magical Thinking for the stage. It premiered on Broadway at the Booth Theatre, with Vanessa Redgrave as Didion. What I haven’t stopped thinking about: those shoes waiting for someone who will never wear them again.

8
'The Brief Wondrous Life of Oscar Wao' by Junot Díaz (2007)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/visionquest-trailer-vision-and-ultron-s-existential-odyssey1-500-x-8441-500-x-844-21.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: The Brief Wondrous Life of Oscar Wao by Junot Diaz

blocks.x: Image via Riverhead Books

At heart, this is a coming-of-age story about an overweight Dominican kid from New Jersey who wants to be the next J.R.R. Tolkien and finally kiss a girl. But Yunior’s unreliable narration keeps getting interrupted by footnotes about dictatorship, migration, masculinity, and Dominican history. Those footnotes make history that normally gets pushed to the bottom of the page keep barging into Oscar’s present.But that's the whole point — Diaz's novel is a textual demonstration of how the past is never gone, and there's no such thing as a single storyline.
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress%2Fwp-content%2Fauthors%2F6aa850b01d393-IMG_2192.jpeg?fit=crop&w=90&h=90

What I remember most is thefukú, the curse supposedly hanging over Oscar’s family and perhaps over the Dominican Republic itself. Is the family cursed, or do people simply inherit the consequences of what came before them? What I haven't stopped thinking about: footnotes. To this day, whenever I’m writing something, I’m looking for an excuse to add a one. Even — especially — in emails.

looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in

fought anyway, by people who will never see how it ends.

You are drawn to grandeur, to white cities and deep forges and the sense that almost
everything you touch is older than your entire family line.

every quiet scene in it a slightly unbearable weight.

you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is
finding out what is over there.

each want something impossible and have decided to go and get it together.

You collect people. Your ideal crew is a set of misfits who were each written off
somewhere else before you turned up and offered them a better idea.

harder because of that rather than in spite of it.

Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the
people are where it all gets complicated.

7
'The Known World' by Edward P. Jones (2003)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/teknown-1.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
Image via Amistad Press

Twenty-three years later, and I may tear up all over again. Edward P. Jones begins with a fact about American slavery that many readers still find startling: Henry Townsend is a Black man in antebellum Virginia who has enslaved Black people. From there, The Known World moves among enslaved and free Black people, their neighboring white landowners, families, and descendants, jumping through time as though the narrator already knows everybody’s ending.

Nobody gets to remain simply innocent or evil. People love one another, betray one another, gain power, misuse it, survive, and sometimes help maintain the very system crushing them. What I haven’t stopped thinking about: a husband and wife escaping a plantation, only for the wife to be kidnapped and sold back into slavery. And his repeated attempts to find her.

6
'Invisible Child' by Andrea Elliott (2021)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/visionquest-trailer-vision-and-ultron-s-existential-odyssey1-500-x-8441-500-x-844-22.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
Image via Random House

Andrea Elliott began reporting on Dasani Coates when she was 11 years old and living with her parents and seven siblings in a Brooklyn homeless shelter. Then Elliott did something most reporters don’t: she stayed. Over the next decade, Elliott follows Dasani through shelters, schools, foster care, addiction, and government agencies supposedly designed to help her family stay secure and intact.

Instead, what Dasani, Elliott, and the readers learn over and over again is how hard it is to be a family when such systems keep breaking them up. Dasani is funny, furious, ambitious, loving, protective, and sometimes impossible. She gets to be a child rather than a symbol of childhood poverty. And the institutions around her seem to be very, very good at documenting her family’s problems without ever actually solving them. What I haven’t stopped thinking about: Dasani’s stepfather repeatedly reporting a broken sink, only for social services to later fail his home inspection because the plumbing didn’t work.

5
'Salvage the Bones' by Jesmyn Ward (2011)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/salvage-the-bones-book0.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
Image via Bloomsbury USA

We know Hurricane Katrina is coming. The Batiste family does not. Salvage the Bones follows 15-year-old Esch and her brothers in rural Mississippi during the days before the storm. Their mother is gone, their father drinks, their home is crumbling, and Esch has discovered she is pregnant by a boy who doesn't really care. And then there's her sweet brother, Skeetah, who's obsessed with his pit bull, China, and her new puppies.

The Batistes are poor, but poverty is not all that is happening to them. They are jealous, lustful, competitive, loving, reckless, and fiercely loyal. And then Katrina arrives. The storm does not create their vulnerability. It makes that vulnerability impossible to ignore. What I haven’t stopped thinking about: Young Skeetah searching for his puppies in the hurricane.

4
'Say Nothing: A True Story of Murder and Memory in Northern Ireland' by Patrick Radden Keefe (2018)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2022/09/say-large0.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
Image via Vintage

I picked up Say Nothing while traveling in Leeds, knowing very little about The Troubles. I figured a huge nonfiction book would keep me occupied for two weeks. Reader, I sat down Friday evening and barely got up until Sunday. Jean McConville, a Belfast mother of 10, is kidnapped from her home in 1972 and never seen again. Her disappearance takes Keefe through the IRA, British soldiers, informants, activists, prisoners, politicians, and decades of violence.

The book moves like a thriller (it was adapted into a Hulu series in 2024 featuring the incredible Lola Petticrew), especially when you remember none of this was invented for suspense. Its title comes from Irish Nobel laureate Seamus Heaney's poem Whatever You Say, Say Nothing, and silence, indeed, hangs over everything: what can be said, what must stay hidden, and who gets to decide what the past officially was. What I haven’t stopped thinking about: Dolours and Marian Price being force-fed during their prison hunger strike.

3
'The Overstory' by Richard Powers (2018)

Richard Powers has a knack for making ordinary relationships feel almost sacred, which makes sense for a novel about trees. Except The Overstory is also not really a novel about trees. Several seemingly unrelated characters eventually converge around chestnuts, redwoods, pines, and entire forests — ecosystems that existed long before any of them and may continue long after.

I genuinely have not looked at trees the same way since reading it. Powers takes something we usually treat as scenery and changes the scale. Suddenly, trees are communities, archives, communication systems — living things operating on a timeline that makes human urgency look a little ridiculous. What I haven’t stopped thinking about: the woman who lives in a tree to keep it from being cut down, inspired by the true story of activist Julia Butterfly Hill.

2
'Pachinko' by Min Jin Lee (2017)

Pachinko follows four generations of a Korean family, beginning with Sunja, who becomes pregnant by a wealthy married man and eventually emigrates to Japan. From there, Min Jin Lee builds a family story around colonialism, migration, poverty, ambition, and anti-Korean discrimination. But the characters are too busy living to behave like representatives of broad historical forces.

Sunja makes decisions because of what seems urgent in the moment. But what's in the moment can change entire timelines for others. Sunja's children inherit the consequences of her seemingly small choices, and their children inherit different versions of the same problems. History keeps changing the rules, while the family keeps trying to make a life anyway. In 2022, Apple TV adapted the novel into a critically acclaimed series that ran for two seasons. What I haven’t stopped thinking about: how one seemingly immediate decision can quietly become the architecture of several generations.

1
'The Underground Railroad' by Colson Whitehead (2016)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/the-underground-railroad-book0.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
Image via Doubleday
https://static0.colliderimages.com/assets/images/sr-db-logo-icon-colored-dark.svg?v=1.9

This book, this book! Colson Whitehead takes the Underground Railroad and makes its metaphor literal: trains, conductors, stations, tracks beneath the country transporting those escaping slavery. Cora escapes a Georgia plantation and travels through states offering different versions of America’s racial nightmare.

One stop seems to be progressive until we learn it is quietly sterilizing Black people. Another has all but eliminated its Black population through terror campaigns. Every stop changes the rules. Whitehead turns American history into a landscape Cora (and the reader) must physically travel through. And because we know the history Cora does not yet know, there is something horrific about watching her move through it. In 2021, Barry Jenkins adapted the novel into a wildly successful series on Amazon. What I haven’t stopped thinking about: Cora stepping off that train at her final stop.

Twenty-three years later, and I may tear up all over again. Edward P. Jones begins with a fact about American slavery that many readers still find startling: Henry Townsend is a Black man in antebellum Virginia who has enslaved Black people. From there, The Known World moves among enslaved and free Black people, their neighboring white landowners, families, and descendants, jumping through time as though the narrator already knows everybody’s ending.

Nobody gets to remain simply innocent or evil. People love one another, betray one another, gain power, misuse it, survive, and sometimes help maintain the very system crushing them. What I haven’t stopped thinking about: a husband and wife escaping a plantation, only for the wife to be kidnapped and sold back into slavery. And his repeated attempts to find her.

6
'Invisible Child' by Andrea Elliott (2021)

Image via Random House

Andrea Elliott began reporting on Dasani Coates when she was 11 years old and living with her parents and seven siblings in a Brooklyn homeless shelter. Then Elliott did something most reporters don’t: she stayed. Over the next decade, Elliott follows Dasani through shelters, schools, foster care, addiction, and government agencies supposedly designed to help her family stay secure and intact.

Instead, what Dasani, Elliott, and the readers learn over and over again is how hard it is to be a family when such systems keep breaking them up. Dasani is funny, furious, ambitious, loving, protective, and sometimes impossible. She gets to be a child rather than a symbol of childhood poverty. And the institutions around her seem to be very, very good at documenting her family’s problems without ever actually solving them. What I haven’t stopped thinking about: Dasani’s stepfather repeatedly reporting a broken sink, only for social services to later fail his home inspection because the plumbing didn’t work.

5
'Salvage the Bones' by Jesmyn Ward (2011)

Image via Bloomsbury USA

We know Hurricane Katrina is coming. The Batiste family does not. Salvage the Bones follows 15-year-old Esch and her brothers in rural Mississippi during the days before the storm. Their mother is gone, their father drinks, their home is crumbling, and Esch has discovered she is pregnant by a boy who doesn't really care. And then there's her sweet brother, Skeetah, who's obsessed with his pit bull, China, and her new puppies.

The Batistes are poor, but poverty is not all that is happening to them. They are jealous, lustful, competitive, loving, reckless, and fiercely loyal. And then Katrina arrives. The storm does not create their vulnerability. It makes that vulnerability impossible to ignore. What I haven’t stopped thinking about: Young Skeetah searching for his puppies in the hurricane.

4
'Say Nothing: A True Story of Murder and Memory in Northern Ireland' by Patrick Radden Keefe (2018)

Image via Vintage

I picked up Say Nothing while traveling in Leeds, knowing very little about The Troubles. I figured a huge nonfiction book would keep me occupied for two weeks. Reader, I sat down Friday evening and barely got up until Sunday. Jean McConville, a Belfast mother of 10, is kidnapped from her home in 1972 and never seen again. Her disappearance takes Keefe through the IRA, British soldiers, informants, activists, prisoners, politicians, and decades of violence.

The book moves like a thriller (it was adapted into a Hulu series in 2024 featuring the incredible Lola Petticrew), especially when you remember none of this was invented for suspense. Its title comes from Irish Nobel laureate Seamus Heaney's poem Whatever You Say, Say Nothing, and silence, indeed, hangs over everything: what can be said, what must stay hidden, and who gets to decide what the past officially was. What I haven’t stopped thinking about: Dolours and Marian Price being force-fed during their prison hunger strike.

3
'The Overstory' by Richard Powers (2018)

Richard Powers has a knack for making ordinary relationships feel almost sacred, which makes sense for a novel about trees. Except The Overstory is also not really a novel about trees. Several seemingly unrelated characters eventually converge around chestnuts, redwoods, pines, and entire forests — ecosystems that existed long before any of them and may continue long after.

I genuinely have not looked at trees the same way since reading it. Powers takes something we usually treat as scenery and changes the scale. Suddenly, trees are communities, archives, communication systems — living things operating on a timeline that makes human urgency look a little ridiculous. What I haven’t stopped thinking about: the woman who lives in a tree to keep it from being cut down, inspired by the true story of activist Julia Butterfly Hill.

2
'Pachinko' by Min Jin Lee (2017)

Pachinko follows four generations of a Korean family, beginning with Sunja, who becomes pregnant by a wealthy married man and eventually emigrates to Japan. From there, Min Jin Lee builds a family story around colonialism, migration, poverty, ambition, and anti-Korean discrimination. But the characters are too busy living to behave like representatives of broad historical forces.

Sunja makes decisions because of what seems urgent in the moment. But what's in the moment can change entire timelines for others. Sunja's children inherit the consequences of her seemingly small choices, and their children inherit different versions of the same problems. History keeps changing the rules, while the family keeps trying to make a life anyway. In 2022, Apple TV adapted the novel into a critically acclaimed series that ran for two seasons. What I haven’t stopped thinking about: how one seemingly immediate decision can quietly become the architecture of several generations.

1
'The Underground Railroad' by Colson Whitehead (2016)

Image via Doubleday

This book, this book! Colson Whitehead takes the Underground Railroad and makes its metaphor literal: trains, conductors, stations, tracks beneath the country transporting those escaping slavery. Cora escapes a Georgia plantation and travels through states offering different versions of America’s racial nightmare.

One stop seems to be progressive until we learn it is quietly sterilizing Black people. Another has all but eliminated its Black population through terror campaigns. Every stop changes the rules. Whitehead turns American history into a landscape Cora (and the reader) must physically travel through. And because we know the history Cora does not yet know, there is something horrific about watching her move through it. In 2021, Barry Jenkins adapted the novel into a wildly successful series on Amazon. What I haven’t stopped thinking about: Cora stepping off that train at her final stop.
